questions.q: What is the defining difference between indirect prompt injection and the direct prompt injection covered in Lesson 5?
options: Indirect injection only affects models that have been fine-tuned, never base models
The malicious instructions are planted in content the model retrieves and processes on someone's behalf, rather than typed into the chat box by the end user
Indirect injection requires the attacker to already have database credentials
Indirect injection is purely theoretical and has no real ingestion path in production systems
questions.explain: It's the same underlying weakness exploited through a different route: a web page, document, or email the system later retrieves, rather than the user's own typed message.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in this lesson as a real ingestion path for indirect prompt injection?
options: A browsing agent summarizing a fetched web page
An email-triage assistant reading an inbox on the user's behalf
A RAG pipeline pulling document chunks into the model's context
A hardware firmware update applied directly to the model's GPU
questions.explain: RAG retrieval, browsing agents, and email/document assistants are all real ingestion paths called out in the lesson. A GPU firmware update has nothing to do with how text reaches the model's context window.

questions.q: Why does OWASP treat indirect prompt injection as arguably the more dangerous subtype of LLM01?
options: It breaks the assumption that an application is only at risk from what its own users type, since the end user can be completely innocent and unaware
It is the only subtype that OWASP officially recognizes at all
It cannot occur unless the model has internet access enabled
It always targets the model's training data directly rather than its runtime input
questions.explain: Indirect injection defeats a common assumption: that only direct user input needs to be treated as untrusted. The legitimate user never has to do anything wrong for the system to be compromised.

questions.q: Why is indirect prompt injection specifically harder to catch than direct injection, according to this lesson?
options: It is encrypted end-to-end so no filter can ever inspect it
It always occurs outside business hours when fewer analysts are monitoring logs
It travels through a retrieval step most teams built to move data rather than treat as an untrusted input channel, so a content filter watching only user messages never sees it
Indirect injection is actually easier to catch than direct injection, not harder
questions.explain: A filter tuned to review the user's chat turn never sees the paragraph sitting inside a retrieved PDF or web page — the injection rides in through a channel that wasn't built to be treated as untrusted.

questions.q: What practical change does this lesson recommend for investigating an LLM application's unexpected behavior?
options: Assume the behavior is a model hallucination and take no further action
Only review the end user's typed messages, since that is always where the root cause will be found
Disable the application's retrieval and browsing features permanently
Ask what content the model retrieved right before it acted unexpectedly, not just what the user typed in that turn
questions.explain: An action with no clear link back to the user's actual request, right after a retrieval or browsing step, is a strong signal worth tracing back to the source content that was ingested.
